answer: History and maturation are two distinct threats that both let improvement look like causation when it is not. History refers to external events occurring alongside a program, such as a new state coverage mandate or COVID-19 shifting utilization, while maturation refers to outcomes that change naturally over time regardless of any intervention. In the tutorial's example, preventive screening rates rose 2.1% annually before a 2020 program and 2.3% after, an added effect of only about 0.2% that falls within noise, indicating the pre-existing trend rather than the program drove the change.

faqs.q: What is the difference between history and maturation threats?
faqs.a: History involves external events that coincide with the program, like a new insurer mandate or a pandemic, while maturation involves outcomes that drift over time on their own, such as growing public awareness. Both can make a program look effective when it is not.

faqs.q: How can a pre-existing trend disguise a program effect?
faqs.a: If an outcome was already rising before the program, continued improvement afterward may simply be that trend continuing. The tutorial shows a pre-program slope of 2.1% per year and a post-program slope of 2.3%, an added effect within noise.

faqs.q: What does an added effect within noise mean?
faqs.a: It means the difference between the pre-program and post-program trends, about 0.2% per year in the tutorial, is too small to distinguish from random variation, so it does not provide credible evidence that the program changed the outcome.
